  ```go
  eng, err := migrate.NewEngine(drv, dir, migrate.WithDialect(pg), migrate.WithGoMigrations(g))
  if err != nil { /* ... */ }
  if _, err := eng.Apply(ctx, migrate.ApplyOptions{}); err != nil { /* ... */ }
  ```

  Use that binary for `apply`, and keep the CLI for `diff`, `hash`, `validate`
  and `drift`.

## 7. Adopting an existing database

Worked example: `examples/adopt-existing-schema`.

`momo generate --from-db` reads a live PostgreSQL database and writes the
models and the init snapshot, so nothing has to be written by hand first.

1. Run `momo generate --from-db DATABASE_URL`. The value is a database URL, `-`
   to read the URL from standard input, or the name of an environment variable
   that holds it; prefer the last two, because a URL on the command line is
   visible in the process list. It inspects the schemas named by
   `migrate.schemas` (default: the current schema), writes one
   `<table>_model.go` per table into the model package (`--out`, else
   `introspect.out`, else the first local entry of `packages`, else `./models`)
   and, when the migration directory has no snapshot, the init migration and
   snapshot. Do not apply the init migration.
2. Run `momo generate`, which writes the generated code for the new models.
3. `momo migrate baseline --version <init version>`. It checks the live
   database against that snapshot, including view, policy and trigger text, and
   exits 1 with `differing object kinds: ...` on a mismatch, then records every
   migration up to that version as `applied` with `statements_applied = 0` and
   `apply_id = baseline`, without running them. `--force` records anyway; use it
   only after reviewing the mismatch. Schema objects outside the models, such as
   extra extensions, count as a mismatch: add them to `migrate.exclude`. The
   run prints a hint for the extensions and skipped tables it found.
4. From then on use `diff` and `apply`.

The models carry exact table and column names (a `table` or `column` tag is
written wherever the naming preset would derive another name), Go types,
nullability (a pointer, or the `nullable` tag for slices), defaults, `size`,
`precision` and `scale`, enums, primary keys, identity (`identity` or
`identity:always`) and serial columns,
single-column indexes as tags, other indexes, unique constraints, checks and
comments in the `MomoConfig` method, every foreign key the generator can
derive as a `belongs_to` field with its `on_delete` and `on_update` actions
(with `fk_name` when the constraint name is not `<table>_<column>_fkey`;
PostgreSQL picks `_fkey1` on a partitioned table), and every composite
(multi-column) foreign key to a modeled table as a `c.ForeignKey(...)`
statement in `MomoConfig`. A composite primary key whose
column order differs from the field order is declared with
`c.PrimaryKey(&m.Name, &m.Scope, &m.At)` in `MomoConfig`; the DDL, inspection
and baseline keep that order. Changing the order of an existing key later is a
drop and add of the primary key under an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock, and the drop
is gated as destructive.
`numeric` columns are Go strings (the `decimal-as-string` note); an
`introspect.types` rule picks a decimal type instead. `tsvector` columns become
`types.TSVector` (`*types.TSVector` when nullable); an `introspect.types` rule
still overrides that.

`momo generate` leaves out type errors that come from files with momo's
generated header, since it rewrites them. After you rename or remove a field,
one `momo generate` run regenerates the stale file; an error in a hand-written
file still stops it.

A column type with no Go mapping is an error and nothing is written; add a rule
to the `introspect` section of `momo.yaml`. Constraints the models cannot
declare are left out of the models and the snapshot and printed as warnings, so
the two agree and the baseline reports them: foreign keys to a table with no
model, single-column foreign keys whose name is not table, column and `_fkey` or
that do not reference a single-column primary key, expression keys with an order or operator class, generated
columns, and PostgreSQL
schemas other than the current one.

### The introspect section

`momo.yaml` holds what the database cannot say, and it is applied again on every
run:

```yaml
introspect:
  package: models # default: the directory name
  out: ./models # default: the first local entry of packages
  skip: ["_prisma_*"] # table globs: no model, not in the snapshot
  types: # SQL type to Go type, for every column of that type
    inet: { go: string }
    numeric(12,2):
      { go: decimal.Decimal, import: github.com/shopspring/decimal }
  columns: # first to last; later rules win, tags add up
    - match: "*.updated_at" # glob over table.column
      tags: [updated_at]
    - match: "users.settings"
      go: "types.JSON[Settings]"
      name: Prefs # Go field name
  tables:
    users: { name: Account, tags: ["soft_delete:timestamp"] }
```

A rule's `tags` are momo tag options; one with the key of a generated option
replaces it. A Go type needs no `import` for `types.`, `vector.`, `time.`,
`json.` or `sql.`. Add skipped tables to `migrate.exclude` too, so the baseline
ignores the live tables.

### Running it again

The schema keeps changing during a port. A re-run rewrites the model files that
nobody edited. Each file starts with a header that holds the hash of its body:
when the body still matches, the file is regenerated freely. A file with hand
edits, or one that `--from-db` did not write, is never replaced. A hand-edited
file stays quiet while the database has not changed its model; it conflicts
only when the regenerated model differs. The run writes
the regenerated version next to it as `<file>.new`, prints
`conflict: <file>`, and exits 1; merge the two by hand and delete the `.new`
file, or run again with `--overwrite` to take the regenerated one.
`--overwrite` only replaces a conflicting file: an edited file whose model the
database did not change stays as it is. A file whose
table is gone is printed as `orphan` and never deleted. `--check` writes
nothing, prints `stale: <file>` for each difference and exits 1. The init
snapshot is written once: when the migration directory already has a snapshot,
use `diff` for later schema changes. Put code of your own in other files and
rules in the `introspect` section, and a re-run stays quiet.

`baseline` needs `CREATE` on the database for the canonicalization step when
the snapshot has views, functions, triggers or policies, **or any table with
text PostgreSQL rewrites**: a column default or generation expression, a check
constraint, an index predicate or an index expression. A snapshot of plain
tables, columns, keys and plain indexes needs no such privilege
(`TestBaselineAsAppRole`). `--force` does not waive it: the error is
`ErrCanonicalizePrivilege`, naming the privilege, and nothing is recorded
(`TestBaselineAsAppRoleNeedsCreateForTableText`). Run the baseline once as a
role that has `CREATE` on the database (for example the owner role), or grant it
for that run. It takes the lock and refuses on dirty or checksum problems like
`apply`.

### Roles and extensions (verified)

Checked on CI with a role that is not a superuser and has no `CREATE` on the
database:

- `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector` **succeeds** when the extension
  already exists (PostgreSQL only emits a notice; it checks existence before
  privileges). So the statement that a generated migration emits is harmless for
  that role once a superuser has installed pgvector
  (`TestAppRoleExtensionIfNotExists`). When the extension is not installed the
  statement needs a privileged role, as before.
- `baseline` and `apply` run `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` for the history table.
  PostgreSQL checks `CREATE` on the schema before it looks for the table, so a
  role with only `USAGE` on the schema is refused with the error
  `permission denied for schema` even when it owns an existing
  `momo_migrations` (`TestBaselineAsAppRoleNeedsCreateOnSchema`). The migrator role needs `CREATE`
  on its schema: `GRANT CREATE ON SCHEMA app TO app_role`.
- With `CREATE` on the schema but not on the database, `baseline` works for a
  snapshot without table text (`TestBaselineAsAppRole`) and fails with
  `ErrCanonicalizePrivilege` otherwise (section 7). `drift` fails with it when
  the snapshot declares a view, a trigger `WHEN` or a policy expression, and
  runs without it for table text only, listing the tables in
  `CanonicalizeSkipped` (`TestDriftBodiesNeedCreateOnDatabase`,
  `TestDriftTablesOnlyRunsAsApplicationRole`).

### Extensions managed outside momo

Set `migrate.external_extensions` in `momo.yaml` for an extension that a
superuser installs by hand:

```yaml
migrate:
  external_extensions: [vector]
```

Names are exact. For each listed extension momo

- never emits `CREATE EXTENSION` from `diff` (or `AutoMigrate`), even when a
  model has a `vector` column, and keeps it out of the snapshot it writes;
- does not report it from `drift`, and does not count it as a mismatch in
  `baseline`, even though the live database has it.

The migrations then no longer create the extension, so a new environment must
get it before the first `apply`. Use it only when that is the intent. It differs
from `migrate.exclude`, which hides unmanaged objects of every kind from drift
and baseline but does not stop `diff` from emitting `CREATE EXTENSION` for a
model that needs it. If a snapshot already declares the extension, the setting
hides it on both sides, so no drop or create is generated either.

A database that uses `serial` or `bigserial` ids is adopted with the `serial`
tag, as in `pk,serial` on an `int64` field. The tag renders `smallserial`,
`serial` or `bigserial` by the Go integer width. Inspection reads a column
whose default is `nextval` of a sequence owned by the column back as the same
serial column, so the snapshot matches and `diff` stays empty. `serial` is
PostgreSQL only; other dialects refuse it. Turning an existing column into or
out of serial is refused by `diff`, with an error that asks for a
hand-written migration.

Upgrade note: inspection used to report a serial column as `identity`. If you
adopted a serial database with `pk,identity` on the model, or kept a snapshot
taken from one, `diff` now stops with `column "id" is a serial column in the
database but the model declares identity`. Change the tag to `pk,serial` and
regenerate the snapshot; or write a migration that converts the column to
identity. Momo does not treat the two as equal, because a new environment
would then be built with identity while production keeps its serial.

`AutoMigrate` is a Go API for development and tests. It applies additive
changes only, writes no history and no files, and returns the rest as
`Skipped`. Do not mix it with versioned migrations on one schema.

## 7a. Cutover from Prisma `db push` to momo

Playbook for a database whose schema is changed by `prisma db push` and
hand-written idempotent SQL files (`DO $$ ... IF NOT EXISTS` guards, `GRANT`
lines, a hand-created extension), moving to momo owning the DDL. Rehearse every
step on a copy of production.

1. **Models first.** Write the momo models so they match the live database
   (section 7). Columns Prisma generates in the client, such as cuid ids, are
   not in the database; model them as plain columns.
2. **Declare what you do not own.** Put the extension a superuser installs in
   `migrate.external_extensions`. Put tables, views and functions that stay
   outside the models (an analytics schema, an audit table, Prisma's
   `_prisma_migrations`) in `migrate.exclude`. Roles, grants and sequences
   outside a column are not part of the schema model; they stay in hand-written
   SQL.
3. **Write the initial migration.** `momo migrate diff init` against an empty
   directory. Do not apply it. Read the generated SQL: it is what a new
   environment would run, and it must build the schema you have.
4. **Rehearse the baseline** on a copy, with
   `momo migrate baseline --version <init version>`, as a role with `CREATE` on
   the database (section 7). Exit 1
   lists the differing object kinds. Fix the models or `exclude` until it is
   clean. Do not use `--force` to skip a difference you have not read.
5. **Dual-writer period: momo watches, it does not write.** While Prisma still
   pushes, the database moves under momo. Do not baseline production yet and do
   not apply migrations. Run `momo migrate drift` against a baselined copy, or
   the rehearsal in step 4 against production, on a schedule. A table Prisma
   added shows as `unmanaged:`, a new column in a managed table as
   `changed: ... not in snapshot`, and an altered column as `changed:`. Each is
   a task: put it in the models, or in `exclude`. Drift cannot see changed view,
   trigger or policy text (section 1).
6. **Freeze `db push`.** Stop `prisma db push` in every environment (remove it
   from the deploy). Update the models to the final live state and, since
   nothing was applied, delete the unapplied `init` files and run `diff init`
   again, so the initial snapshot is the schema as it is at the freeze.
7. **Baseline each environment.** In each environment run
   `momo migrate baseline --version <init version>` once, then
   `momo migrate drift` (expect `no drift`). The role that runs `apply` needs
   `CREATE` on the schema (section 7). From then on `apply` runs only newer
   migrations. A database created from scratch runs the init migration; it needs
   the external extension installed first.
8. **Hand off.** Schema changes go through `diff`; backfills and other data
   changes through `momo migrate new --custom`, which replaces the hand-written
   SQL files. Leave guards such as `IF NOT EXISTS` out of new files: the
   history says what ran.

Undo: baseline only writes history rows, so drop the `momo_migrations` table to
return to the state before step 7; nothing else changed.

## 8. Security

- `momo` redacts connection strings from everything it prints (stdout, stderr,
  error text, and bad flag values that a pasted URL lands in): URL userinfo
  becomes `***@`, a URL in text that has a query keeps the part before `?` and
  shows `?***`, a `password=`/`passwd=`/`pwd=` value becomes `***`, and the
  exact URL and password given are replaced by `***`.
  History `error` text is the server message only, never `Detail`. Messages of
  SQLSTATE class 22 (data exception) are withheld because they can contain
  data values. Connection URLs and `password=` values in the text are replaced
  by `***` before it is stored (`TestHistoryErrorIsRedacted`).
- A warning on stderr (not a failure) when a command that needs a database is
  given a URL with `sslmode=disable` and any non-local host:
  `TLS is not enforced (sslmode=disable) for remote host H: credentials and data can cross the network unencrypted; use sslmode=verify-full`.
  It names the hosts only. It also fires when the URL or key=value string has
  no `sslmode` (libpq then uses `prefer`, which falls back to plaintext), for
  `allow` and `prefer`, for key=value connection strings, and when `sslmode`
  comes from `PGSSLMODE`; a host missing from the string is read from
  `PGHOST`. `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, unix socket paths and no host at
  all do not warn, and neither do `require`, `verify-ca` and `verify-full`.
  `require` encrypts but does not check the server's identity, so use
  `sslmode=verify-full` against a real server.
- Do not pass the URL with `--url` on shared hosts (momo warns); use
  `migrate.url_env`, `MOMO_DATABASE_URL` or `--url -` (stdin).
- Review `*.up.sql` in code review like any code: `apply` runs it as the
  connected role, and `momo.sum` only detects change, not intent.
- Tamper detection is against accidental edits, not an attacker.
  `momo migrate hash` rewrites `momo.sum` to match whatever is on disk, and
  `momo migrate rehash --accept` stores the checksum of whatever file is on
  disk in the history row. Both trust the files completely: anyone who can edit the
  migration files and run those commands can make an edited migration pass
  every check. Protect the migration directory with code review and write
  access control, and the database with the migrator role's grants; `momo.sum`
  does not.
- `drift` and `baseline` execute model DDL on the target database. To compare
  declared text with what the database reports, they create a scratch schema
  and run the declared definitions (defaults, checks, index predicates, view
  queries, function bodies, policy and trigger expressions) in a transaction
  that is rolled back. That needs `CREATE` on the database, runs SQL taken
  from your snapshots and models, and takes locks while it runs. Run them
  against a scratch database restored from a backup, or a clone, rather than
  production.

## 9. MySQL and MariaDB

The `migrate/mysql` package is the migration dialect for MySQL 8.4, MySQL 9.7
and MariaDB 11.8. It reads `information_schema`, renders DDL and locks with
`GET_LOCK`. `momo migrate` does not select it yet; build the engine with
`migrate.WithDialect(mmysql.New())` and the `mysqldriver` driver.

**Every migration is non-transactional.** DDL implies a commit on these
servers, so a failure cannot be rolled back. The engine runs each statement on
its own, records `statements_applied` after each one, and leaves a failed row
that is dirty until you repair the database and run `resolve`. This holds with
or without `-- momo:no-transaction`, for Go migrations, and for `rollback`: a
down that fails half-way leaves its earlier statements applied and the row
failed. Write each
migration so that a half-applied run is easy to finish by hand.

**Locking.** `GET_LOCK` names are server-wide, so the lock name carries the
database (`momo:<database>.momo_migrations`, cut to the 64 characters MySQL
allows, with a hash suffix when the key is longer). The lock belongs to the
pinned connection and is released with `RELEASE_LOCK`, or when the connection
ends. A busy lock returns `migrate.ErrLocked` with the connection id of the
holder.

**Session timeouts.** The lock timeout becomes `lock_wait_timeout`, the time a
statement waits for a metadata lock, in whole seconds. A statement timeout
becomes `max_statement_time` on MariaDB; on MySQL it is refused with
`momo.ErrUnsupported`, because `max_execution_time` bounds SELECT only.

**Online DDL.** A line `-- momo:ddl ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE` directly
before an `ALTER TABLE` statement appends those options to it. MySQL rejects
`LOCK=NONE` together with `ALGORITHM=INSTANT`; use `ALGORITHM=INSTANT` alone. The server
rejects the statement when it cannot honour them, so a change that would copy
the table fails instead of running slowly. Without the directive momo adds no
`ALGORITHM` or `LOCK` clause. Only `ALGORITHM=` and `LOCK=` options are
accepted.

**What inspection reports.** One database is inspected, the connection's
default, and the history table is left out.

- A UNIQUE constraint and a unique index are the same object on these servers.
  A unique key made of plain ascending columns is reported as a unique
  constraint; declare such keys as constraints.
- The index MySQL creates for a foreign key, named after the constraint, is
  not reported, and the diff refuses a declared index that has the name of a
  foreign key of its table, because the two would collide and could not be
  told apart. An index of a database you adopt that already has such a name
  and the key's columns is treated as the server's own.
- `NO ACTION` is reported as an empty action. MariaDB reports its default as
  `RESTRICT`, so on MariaDB `RESTRICT` and an unwritten clause are one.
- MariaDB stores `json` as `longtext` with a `json_valid` check named after the
  column; the pair is reported as type `json`.
- A column is reported with a collation only when it differs from its table's
  default; declare `Collate` on the column to pin one.
- Defaults that the servers store alike are one default: `NOW`, `LOCALTIME`
  and `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`; `TRUE` and `FALSE` are `1` and `0`. `RESTRICT` and
  `NO ACTION` are the same foreign key action.
- Stored CHECK text is compared without the identifier quotes, character set
  introducers and the parentheses MySQL adds around each comparison. Other
  rewrites by the server (for example `!=` stored as `<>`) show as a
  difference of text; write the expression the way the server stores it.
  Parentheses around a comparison are removed only between and, or and xor,
  so `(a between 1 and 2) and c > 0` keeps them and differs from the same
  text without them; a backslash escape inside a string is kept as written.
- A foreign key into another database is reported as `database.table`.
- Integer display widths (`int(11)` on MariaDB) are no difference of type.
  Identifier quotes, character set introducers and outer parentheses in stored
  expressions are no difference of text.
- An index part with a prefix length is the column name followed by the length
  in parentheses, such as `name(10)`. Index visibility, character sets and
  `ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` are not part of the schema model, and a
  `MODIFY COLUMN` that a type change renders restates the column without them:
  an `ALTER` of such a column is a migration to write by hand.

**Rendering.** Tables are `ENGINE=InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET=utf8mb4`. An identity
column is `AUTO_INCREMENT` (`by_default`; `always` and `serial` are refused). A
default that is not a literal or `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` is wrapped in parentheses,
as MySQL requires. Partial indexes, storage parameters, operator classes,
enums, views, functions, triggers and policies have no MySQL rendering yet and
are refused. The `hash` index method is refused: InnoDB builds it as BTREE. Dropping a
foreign key also drops the index MySQL built for it, when one exists, unless
another foreign key of the table starts with the same column: that key may rely
on the index, and dropping it would fail after the key was gone. The index then
stays and shows as an index named like the dropped key; declare it, or drop it
once nothing needs it. An
AUTO_INCREMENT column must be a key in the statement that adds it, but the
engine adds a primary key in a separate statement after the column: add such a
column and its key in a migration you write yourself. Declare a generated
column as nullable: MariaDB does not take
`NOT NULL` on one. MySQL refuses a CHECK, or a stored generated column, on a
column that a foreign key with a referential action uses.

## Upgrading: generated file header

Generated Go files start with `// Code generated by momo (format 1). DO NOT EDIT.`.
The header carries the generated-file format number, which decides
compatibility, and no momo release version, so a later momo upgrade does not
rewrite generated files whose code is unchanged. Earlier releases wrote the
same line with a release version between `momo` and `(format 1)`; momo still
recognises that form, so orphan detection keeps working.

After upgrading, run `momo generate` once. Until then `momo generate --check`
reports the header change in every generated file.

## Known issues

None open. Fixed issues are listed in the changelog.


# Source: importers.md

# Importing models from other ORMs

Momo can read the models of an existing GORM, Bun or Ent project and write the
equivalent Momo structs. Three packages do the reading:

| Package         | Reads                                                     |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `importer/gorm` | GORM structs and their `gorm:"..."` tags, `gorm.Model`    |
| `importer/bun`  | Bun structs and their `bun:"..."` tags                    |
| `importer/ent`  | the Ent `schema` package (fields, edges, indexes, mixins) |

Each package exports one function, `Read(dir string)`, that returns the neutral
`[]importer.Model` and an `*importer.Report`. `importer.Emit` turns the models
into Momo source through the generator's writer.

The readers are static. They parse the Go files of `dir` with `go/parser` and
never compile, load or execute your code, so reading a project cannot run its
`init` functions, hooks or migrations. The flip side is that they see only what
is written as a literal in those files: a naming strategy set in another
package, or an index added by a migration, is not visible. Each reader's
package comment lists its limits.

## The `momo import` command

```sh
momo import gorm --src ./old/models --out ./models
momo import bun  --src ./old/models --out ./models --report import-report.txt
momo import ent  --src ./ent/schema --out ./models --package models
```

The command runs the reader, prints the import report to standard output and
writes the Momo structs to `<out>/models.go` with a generated-file header.
`--package` sets the Go package name (the default is derived from `--out`),
and `--report` also writes the report to a file.

Exit codes: `0` the models were written, `1` the report holds an `unsupported`
change and nothing was written, `2` a usage or input error. Fix or convert the
listed constructs by hand, or remove them from the source, and run it again.
The command never overwrites a file that does not carry the generated-file
header.

## Importing migration history

The `importer/history` package converts the migration history of another tool
into a Momo migration directory, so a database that already ran those
migrations does not run them again. Four readers produce the input:

| Package                          | Reads                                                                                             |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `importer/history/atlas`         | an Atlas directory (`<version>_<name>.sql`, `atlas.sum`) and the rows of `atlas_schema_revisions` |
| `importer/history/goose`         | a goose directory and the `goose_db_version` table                                                |
| `importer/history/golangmigrate` | `<version>_<title>.up.sql` and `.down.sql` files and `schema_migrations`                          |
| `importer/history/bun`           | Bun's SQL migrations and the `bun_migrations` table                                               |

Each package exports `Read`, which returns a `history.Source`. `history.Convert`
refuses a source that is dirty, that holds migrations the tool never applied, or
that holds migrations it cannot convert (Bun and goose Go-function migrations).
A source version that is not a 14-digit timestamp is mapped to
`19700101000000` plus its position in the list, and the mapping is reported as a
`version-mapped` change; the original version stays in the history `name`
column. `history.Baseline` replays the converted SQL on an empty scratch
database to write one schema snapshot per migration, `history.WriteImport`
writes the directory and `history.HistoryRows` gives the `momo_migrations` rows
that mark every migration as applied. The Atlas reader verifies `atlas.sum`
with Atlas's directory hash and refuses a directory whose files were edited.
golang-migrate records only its current version, so every migration up to it is
read as applied.

## The import report

A Momo model is never an exact copy of an ORM model, because the ORMs differ in
behaviour you do not see in the struct: GORM replaces a zero value with the
column default, Ent saves an edge only when its setter was called, and so on.
The importer does not paper over these differences. Every one becomes a
`importer.Change` in the report, with the source position (`file:line:col`), the model,
the field and a message. `importer.Report.String()` prints one line per change, sorted by
position, in the form `source: kind: Model.Field: message`.

Read the report before you trust the converted models. `importer.Report.Has(kind)` and
`importer.Report.Of(kind)` filter it in code. The kinds are:

| Kind                  | Meaning                                                                                                                                  |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `zero-value-handling` | the source ORM treats a zero value as unset and applies a default; Momo writes the zero value (use a pointer to leave it unset)          |
| `implicit-save`       | the source ORM saves an association together with its parent; Momo writes only the model you pass                                        |
| `go-default`          | the source ORM computes a default in Go (timestamps, generated values); Momo needs a tag or a database default                           |
| `unsupported`         | something the reader cannot convert (an unreadable tag, an unknown builder call, a type with no mapping); convert it by hand             |
| `renamed-type`        | the field type changes on import, for example `gorm.DeletedAt` becomes `*time.Time`, and the automatic filter does not carry over        |
| `dropped-field`       | a field that does not become a column (ignored with `-`, scan-only, relation fields) is not imported                                     |
| `dropped-index`       | an index Momo's tags cannot express (a composite index, a second index tag on a field) is not imported; declare it in the companion file |
| `naming`              | a table, column, constraint or foreign key name that Momo derives itself, or a naming strategy the reader cannot see; check the names    |
| `version-mapped`      | a migration version was renumbered while importing migration history (`importer/history`)                                                |
| `go-side-rule`        | a validator, immutable field, hook or policy that the source ORM runs in Go and Momo does not                                            |

The importer never drops one of these silently: an empty report means the
reader found nothing to flag, not that it checked behaviour it cannot see.


# Source: guides/gorm.md

# Coming from GORM

This page maps the GORM calls you use every day to their Momo equivalents. It
does not try to hide the differences: Momo writes exactly the SQL of the call
you made, never retries, and never saves more than the model you pass. To
convert existing GORM structs automatically, read
[importing models from other ORMs](../importers.md) (`momo import gorm`).

The programs on this page are compiled against the models of the
[quickstart example](../../examples/quickstart/): an `Author` that has many
`Post` rows. Blocks fenced as `go notest` show code that is not compiled here.

## Cheat sheet

| GORM                                     | Momo                                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `gorm:"primaryKey"`                      | `momo:"pk"`; add `identity` for a generated key                                        |
| `gorm:"size:200;not null;uniqueIndex"`   | `momo:"size:200,notnull,unique"`                                                       |
| `gorm:"column:author_id;index"`          | `momo:"column:author_id,index"`                                                        |
| `db.Where("name = ?", n).Find(&rows)`    | <code>momo.Select&#91;T&#93;(db).Where(col.Eq(n)).All(ctx)</code>                      |
| `db.First(&row, id)`                     | <code>momo.Select&#91;T&#93;(db).Where(col.Eq(id)).One(ctx)</code>                     |
| `db.Create(&row)`                        | <code>momo.Insert&#91;T&#93;(db).Model(&amp;row).Exec(ctx)</code>                      |
| `db.Model(&row).Update("name", n)`       | <code>momo.Update&#91;T&#93;(db).Set(col.Set(n)).Where(...).Exec(ctx)</code>           |
| `db.Delete(&row)`                        | <code>momo.Delete&#91;T&#93;(db).Where(...).Exec(ctx)</code>                           |
| `db.Preload("Posts").Find(&rows)`        | <code>momo.Select&#91;T&#93;(db).Preload(author.Posts).All(ctx)</code>, or `momo.Load` |
| `db.Transaction(func(tx *gorm.DB)...)`   | `db.Tx(ctx, momo.TxOptions{}, func(tx *momo.Tx) error {...})`                          |
| `db.AutoMigrate(&T{})`                   | `momo migrate diff <name>`, then `momo migrate apply`                                  |
| `errors.Is(err, gorm.ErrRecordNotFound)` | `errors.Is(err, momo.ErrNotFound)`                                                     |

## Models

GORM reads struct tags at run time. Momo reads the `momo:` tags and the
optional `MomoConfig` method statically, when you run `momo generate`; the
generator writes typed column handles such as `author.Name`. A Momo struct
embeds `momo.Model`, which carries the table name:

```go notest
type Author struct {
	momo.Model `momo:"table:authors"`
	ID         int64  `momo:"pk,identity"`
	Name       string `momo:"size:200,notnull,unique"`

	Posts []Post `momo:"has_many,fk:AuthorID"`
}
```

Three behaviours differ from GORM and matter when you port a model:

- GORM replaces a zero value with the column default on insert. Momo writes the
  zero value you gave it. Use a pointer field to write NULL or to leave a value
  to the database default.
- GORM treats a field named `ID` as the key and `CreatedAt` and `UpdatedAt` as
  managed timestamps by convention. Momo uses the tags you wrote.
- `gorm.DeletedAt` soft delete becomes an explicit soft-delete field; see the
  [type mapping](../TYPE_MAPPING.md).

`momo import gorm` reports each of these as a change (`zero-value-handling`,
`renamed-type`) with the position of the field.

## Queries

A query is built from typed columns, so a misspelled column or a value of the
wrong type fails to compile. `All` returns every row, `One` returns exactly one
row and fails with `momo.ErrNotFound` when there is none.

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models/post"
)

// recentPosts is db.Where("author_id = ?", id).Order("title").Limit(10).Find(&posts) in GORM.
func recentPosts(ctx context.Context, q momo.Querier, authorID int64) ([]models.Post, error) {
	return momo.Select[models.Post](q).
		Where(post.AuthorID.Eq(authorID)).
		OrderBy(post.Title.Asc()).
		Limit(10).
		All(ctx)
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

	posts, err := recentPosts(ctx, db, 1)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(len(posts), "posts")
}
```

Raw SQL stays available through `momo.Exec` and `momo.Scalars`; `?` binds the
next argument, so a value never becomes part of the SQL text.

## Relations

GORM's `Preload` runs one extra query per relation. So does Momo, and you pick
where it happens: `momo.Load` fills a relation on models you already have, and
`SelectQuery.Preload` attaches the loader to the query so `All`, `One` and
`First` run it for you. Nothing is loaded unless you ask, and a relation is
never saved with its parent; write the children with their own insert.

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models/author"
)

// authorsWithPosts is db.Preload("Posts").Find(&authors) in GORM.
func authorsWithPosts(ctx context.Context, q momo.Querier) ([]models.Author, error) {
	return momo.Select[models.Author](q).Preload(author.Posts).All(ctx)
}

// loadPosts fills Posts on authors you already have.
func loadPosts(ctx context.Context, q momo.Querier, authors []models.Author) error {
	return momo.Load(ctx, q, authors, author.Posts)
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

	authors, err := authorsWithPosts(ctx, db)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	if err := loadPosts(ctx, db, authors); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(len(authors), "authors")
}
```

See [relations](../relations.md) for filtering a loaded relation, joins and
writing related rows.

## Hooks

GORM calls `BeforeCreate`, `BeforeUpdate`, `BeforeDelete` and `AfterFind`
methods on the model. Momo has the same four points as typed functions on the
model's metadata, `HookSet`: `BeforeInsert`, `BeforeUpdate`, `BeforeDelete` and
`AfterLoad`. They are set once at start-up on the `Meta` value, not as methods
on the struct:

```go notest
var authorMeta = momo.Meta[Author]{ /* generated metadata */ Hooks: momo.HookSet[Author]{
	BeforeInsert: func(ctx context.Context, a *Author) error {
		a.Name = strings.TrimSpace(a.Name)
		return nil
	},
}}
```

A hook runs only on the typed execution methods (`Exec`, `All`, `One` and so
on), not on raw SQL, and an error from a Before hook stops the statement before
any SQL runs. Hooks do not run for relations loaded with `Load` or `Preload`.
Per-handle rules such as a tenant filter belong in an
[interceptor](../PRIVACY_RULES.md), which runs before the hooks.

## Transactions

`db.Transaction` in GORM and `db.Tx` in Momo both commit when the function
returns nil and roll back on an error or a panic. Momo calls the function
exactly once: there is no automatic retry, so retry a serialization failure in
your own code. Use the `tx` handle for every statement inside the function.

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models/author"
)

func rename(ctx context.Context, db *momo.DB, id int64, name string) error {
	return db.Tx(ctx, momo.TxOptions{}, func(tx *momo.Tx) error {
		a, err := momo.Select[models.Author](tx).Where(author.ID.Eq(id)).One(ctx)
		if errors.Is(err, momo.ErrNotFound) {
			return fmt.Errorf("author %d does not exist", id)
		}
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		_, err = momo.Update[models.Author](tx).
			Set(author.Name.Set(name)).
			Where(author.ID.Eq(a.ID)).
			Exec(ctx)
		return err
	})
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

	if err := rename(ctx, db, 1, "Ada Lovelace"); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## Migrations

`AutoMigrate` compares your structs with the live database and changes it on
the spot. Momo's `AutoMigrate` Go API also exists, but it only adds (tables,
columns, indexes), writes no history and is meant for development and tests.
For a real database use versioned files:

```sh
momo migrate diff add_authors   # writes <version>_add_authors.up.sql, a snapshot and momo.sum
momo migrate apply              # applies pending files under a lock and records them
momo migrate status
```

If the database already has a schema from GORM, put it under Momo with
`momo migrate baseline` (see [migrations](../migrations.md)); if you ran GORM
inside another tool's migrations, [import that history](../importers.md) so
nothing runs twice.

## Errors

GORM returns `gorm.ErrRecordNotFound` from `First`. Momo classifies database
errors into sentinels you compare with `errors.Is`, never with the error text:
`momo.ErrNotFound` for a single-row call that found nothing,
`momo.ErrUniqueViolation` and `momo.ErrForeignKeyViolation` for constraint
failures. `All` returns an empty slice, not an error, when nothing matches.


# Source: guides/bun.md

# Coming from Bun

This page maps the Bun calls you use every day to their Momo equivalents. Bun
and Momo are both close to SQL, so most calls translate one to one. The
differences are in what Momo does not do for you: it writes exactly the SQL of
the call you made, never retries, and never saves more than the model you pass.
To convert existing Bun structs automatically, read
[importing models from other ORMs](../importers.md) (`momo import bun`).

The programs on this page are compiled against the models of the
[quickstart example](../../examples/quickstart/): an `Author` that has many
`Post` rows. Blocks fenced as `go notest` show code that is not compiled here.

## Cheat sheet

| Bun                                          | Momo                                                          |
| -------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `bun:"table:users,alias:u"` on `BaseModel`   | `momo:"table:users"` on the embedded `momo.Model`             |
| `bun:",pk,autoincrement"`                    | `momo:"pk,identity"`                                          |
| `bun:",notnull,unique"`                      | `momo:"notnull,unique"`                                       |
| `bun:",nullzero"`                            | a pointer field (Momo writes the zero value otherwise)        |
| `bun:"rel:has-many,join:id=author_id"`       | `momo:"has_many,fk:AuthorID"`                                 |
| `bun:"rel:belongs-to,join:author_id=id"`     | `momo:"belongs_to,fk:AuthorID"`                               |
| `NewSelect().Model(&rows).Where(...)`        | `momo.Select[T]` with `Where` and `All`                       |
| `NewInsert().Model(&row).Exec(ctx)`          | `momo.Insert[T]` with `Model` and `Exec`                      |
| `NewUpdate().Model(&row).WherePK()`          | `momo.Update[T]` with `Set`, `Where` and `Exec`               |
| `NewDelete().Model(&row).WherePK()`          | `momo.Delete[T]` with `Where` and `Exec`                      |
| `.Relation("Posts")`                         | `.Preload(author.Posts)` on the select, or `momo.Load`        |
| `db.RunInTx(ctx, nil, func(ctx, tx bun.Tx))` | `db.Tx(ctx, momo.TxOptions{}, func(tx *momo.Tx) error {...})` |
| `bun migrate.NewMigrator(db, migrations)`    | `momo migrate diff <name>`, then `momo migrate apply`         |
| `errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows)`              | `errors.Is(err, momo.ErrNotFound)`                            |

## Models

Bun reads its struct tags at run time through reflection. Momo reads the
`momo:` tags and the optional `MomoConfig` method statically, when you run
`momo generate`; the generator writes typed column handles such as `author.Name`.

```go notest
type Author struct {
	momo.Model `momo:"table:authors"`
	ID         int64  `momo:"pk,identity"`
	Name       string `momo:"size:200,notnull,unique"`

	Posts []Post `momo:"has_many,fk:AuthorID"`
}
```

One behaviour differs from Bun and matters when you port a model: `nullzero`
makes Bun write NULL for a zero value. Momo writes the zero value you gave it;
use a pointer field to write NULL. `momo import bun` reports each `nullzero`
field as `zero-value-handling` and each `default:` as a database default.

## Queries

A query is built from typed columns, so a misspelled column or a value of the
wrong type fails to compile. `All` returns every row, `One` returns exactly one
row and fails with `momo.ErrNotFound` when there is none.

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models/post"
)

// recentPosts is the Momo form of NewSelect().Model(&posts).Where("author_id = ?", id).Order("title").Limit(10).
func recentPosts(ctx context.Context, q momo.Querier, authorID int64) ([]models.Post, error) {
	return momo.Select[models.Post](q).
		Where(post.AuthorID.Eq(authorID)).
		OrderBy(post.Title.Asc()).
		Limit(10).
		All(ctx)
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

	posts, err := recentPosts(ctx, db, 1)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(len(posts), "posts")
}
```

Raw SQL stays available through `momo.Exec` and `momo.Scalars`; `?` binds the
next argument, as in Bun, so a value never becomes part of the SQL text.

## Relations

Bun's `.Relation("Posts")` joins or runs a second query depending on the
relation. Momo always says which: `momo.Load` fills a relation on models you
already have with one extra query, and `SelectQuery.Preload` attaches the loader
to the query so `All`, `One` and `First` run it for you. A relation is never
saved with its parent; write the children with their own insert.

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models/author"
)

// authorsWithPosts is NewSelect().Model(&authors).Relation("Posts") in Bun.
func authorsWithPosts(ctx context.Context, q momo.Querier) ([]models.Author, error) {
	return momo.Select[models.Author](q).Preload(author.Posts).All(ctx)
}

// loadPosts fills Posts on authors you already have.
func loadPosts(ctx context.Context, q momo.Querier, authors []models.Author) error {
	return momo.Load(ctx, q, authors, author.Posts)
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

	authors, err := authorsWithPosts(ctx, db)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	if err := loadPosts(ctx, db, authors); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(len(authors), "authors")
}
```

See [relations](../relations.md) for filtering a loaded relation, joins and
writing related rows.

## Hooks

Bun has model hooks such as `BeforeAppendModel` and query hooks added with
`AddQueryHook`. Momo separates the two. Model hooks are typed functions on the
model's metadata, `HookSet`: `BeforeInsert`, `BeforeUpdate`, `BeforeDelete` and
`AfterLoad`, set once at start-up on the `Meta` value. Observing every
statement is `momo.WithHook`, and per-handle rules such as a tenant filter are
[interceptors](../PRIVACY_RULES.md).

```go notest
var authorMeta = momo.Meta[Author]{ /* generated metadata */ Hooks: momo.HookSet[Author]{
	BeforeInsert: func(ctx context.Context, a *Author) error {
		a.Name = strings.TrimSpace(a.Name)
		return nil
	},
}}
```

A model hook runs only on the typed execution methods (`Exec`, `All`, `One` and
so on), not on raw SQL, and an error from a Before hook stops the statement
before any SQL runs.

## Transactions

`RunInTx` in Bun and `db.Tx` in Momo both commit when the function returns nil
and roll back on an error or a panic. Momo calls the function exactly once:
there is no automatic retry, so retry a serialization failure in your own code.
Use the `tx` handle for every statement inside the function.

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models/author"
)

func rename(ctx context.Context, db *momo.DB, id int64, name string) error {
	return db.Tx(ctx, momo.TxOptions{}, func(tx *momo.Tx) error {
		a, err := momo.Select[models.Author](tx).Where(author.ID.Eq(id)).One(ctx)
		if errors.Is(err, momo.ErrNotFound) {
			return fmt.Errorf("author %d does not exist", id)
		}
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		_, err = momo.Update[models.Author](tx).
			Set(author.Name.Set(name)).
			Where(author.ID.Eq(a.ID)).
			Exec(ctx)
		return err
	})
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

	if err := rename(ctx, db, 1, "Ada Lovelace"); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## Migrations

Bun's migrator runs SQL files or Go functions registered in your program and
records them in `bun_migrations`. Momo's migrations are SQL files that
`momo migrate diff` writes from your models, each with a schema snapshot and a
`momo.sum` checksum file:

```sh
momo migrate diff add_authors   # writes <version>_add_authors.up.sql, a snapshot and momo.sum
momo migrate apply              # applies pending files under a lock and records them
momo migrate status
```

A database that Bun already migrated keeps its schema. Import the SQL
migrations and the `bun_migrations` rows with the Bun history reader
(`importer/history/bun`, see [importing](../importers.md)) so none of them runs
again. Bun migrations written as Go functions cannot be imported; the reader
lists them and refuses the import until you convert them to SQL.

## Errors

Bun returns the driver's error, and `sql.ErrNoRows` from `Scan` on an empty
result. Momo classifies database errors into sentinels you compare with
`errors.Is`, never with the error text: `momo.ErrNotFound` for a single-row call
that found nothing, `momo.ErrUniqueViolation` and `momo.ErrForeignKeyViolation`
for constraint failures. `All` returns an empty slice, not an error, when
nothing matches.


# Source: guides/ent.md

# Coming from Ent

This page maps the Ent calls you use every day to their Momo equivalents. Ent
generates a client from schema code; Momo generates typed column handles from
plain structs. The differences are in what Momo does not do for you: it writes
exactly the SQL of the call you made, never retries, and never saves an edge you
did not write. To convert an existing Ent schema automatically, run
`momo import ent` (see [importing models from other ORMs](../importers.md)): it
reads the schema package with `go/parser` and never compiles or runs it.

The programs on this page are compiled against the models of the
[quickstart example](../../examples/quickstart/): an `Author` that has many
`Post` rows. Blocks fenced as `go notest` show code that is not compiled here.

## Cheat sheet

| Ent                                              | Momo                                                                         |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `field.String("name").NotEmpty().Unique()`       | `Name string` with `momo:"notnull,unique"`                                   |
| `field.String("bio").Optional().Nillable()`      | `Bio *string`                                                                |
| `field.Int64("id")` (the implicit key)           | `ID int64` with `momo:"pk,identity"`                                         |
| `edge.To("posts", Post.Type)`                    | `Posts []Post` with `momo:"has_many,fk:AuthorID"`                            |
| `edge.From("author", Author.Type).Ref("posts")`  | `Author *Author` with `momo:"belongs_to,fk:AuthorID"`                        |
| `client.Author.Query().Where(author.NameEQ(n))`  | <code>momo.Select&#91;T&#93;(db).Where(col.Eq(n)).All(ctx)</code>            |
| `client.Author.Create().SetName(n).Save(ctx)`    | <code>momo.Insert&#91;T&#93;(db).Model(&amp;row).Exec(ctx)</code>            |
| `client.Author.UpdateOneID(id).SetName(n)`       | <code>momo.Update&#91;T&#93;(db).Set(col.Set(n)).Where(...).Exec(ctx)</code> |
| `client.Author.DeleteOneID(id).Exec(ctx)`        | <code>momo.Delete&#91;T&#93;(db).Where(...).Exec(ctx)</code>                 |
| `.WithPosts()` (eager loading)                   | `.Preload(author.Posts)` on the select, or `momo.Load`                       |
| `client.Tx(ctx)`, `tx.Commit()`, `tx.Rollback()` | `db.Tx(ctx, momo.TxOptions{}, func(tx *momo.Tx) error {...})`                |
| `client.Schema.Create(ctx)`                      | `momo migrate diff <name>`, then `momo migrate apply`                        |
| `ent.IsNotFound(err)`                            | `errors.Is(err, momo.ErrNotFound)`                                           |

## Models

Ent describes a table with builder chains in a `Fields` method, and generates a
client and a package of predicates per entity. Momo describes a table as a
struct and generates typed column handles such as `author.Name`, which are the
predicates and setters you use in queries.

```go notest
type Author struct {
	momo.Model `momo:"table:authors"`
	ID         int64  `momo:"pk,identity"`
	Name       string `momo:"size:200,notnull,unique"`

	Posts []Post `momo:"has_many,fk:AuthorID"`
}
```

`momo import ent` converts the fields, edges, indexes, mixins and the
`entsql.Annotation` table name it can read as literals. Anything it cannot read
without running your code (a many-to-many edge, JSON and UUID fields, a custom
key, an unknown builder method) is an `unsupported` change at its `file:line:col`:
nothing is written until you remove or convert it. Two behaviours differ from Ent
and are reported as changes:

- Ent applies a field's `Default` in Go when the setter was not called. Momo
  writes the zero value you gave it (`zero-value-handling`); keep the database
  default with a `default:` tag or a pointer field.
- Ent saves an edge only when its setter was called, and Momo saves a relation
  only when you write it, so `edge.From` with `.Ref` is reported as
  `implicit-save` to make you check the write paths.

## Queries

A query is built from typed columns, so a misspelled column or a value of the
wrong type fails to compile. `All` returns every row, `One` returns exactly one
row and fails with `momo.ErrNotFound` when there is none.

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models/post"
)

// recentPosts is client.Post.Query().Where(post.AuthorID(id)).Order(ent.Asc("title")).Limit(10).All(ctx) in Ent.
func recentPosts(ctx context.Context, q momo.Querier, authorID int64) ([]models.Post, error) {
	return momo.Select[models.Post](q).
		Where(post.AuthorID.Eq(authorID)).
		OrderBy(post.Title.Asc()).
		Limit(10).
		All(ctx)
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

	posts, err := recentPosts(ctx, db, 1)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(len(posts), "posts")
}
```

Raw SQL stays available through `momo.Exec` and `momo.Scalars`; `?` binds the
next argument, so a value never becomes part of the SQL text.

## Relations

Ent loads an edge when you ask with `WithPosts()`, one extra query per edge.
Momo does the same and you pick where it happens: `momo.Load` fills a relation
on models you already have, and `SelectQuery.Preload` attaches the loader to the
query so `All`, `One` and `First` run it for you. A relation is never saved
with its parent; write the children with their own insert.

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models/author"
)

// authorsWithPosts is client.Author.Query().WithPosts().All(ctx) in Ent.
func authorsWithPosts(ctx context.Context, q momo.Querier) ([]models.Author, error) {
	return momo.Select[models.Author](q).Preload(author.Posts).All(ctx)
}

// loadPosts fills Posts on authors you already have.
func loadPosts(ctx context.Context, q momo.Querier, authors []models.Author) error {
	return momo.Load(ctx, q, authors, author.Posts)
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

	authors, err := authorsWithPosts(ctx, db)
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	if err := loadPosts(ctx, db, authors); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(len(authors), "authors")
}
```

See [relations](../relations.md) for filtering a loaded relation, joins and
writing related rows.

## Hooks

Ent hooks wrap mutations (`ent.Hook`, added with `client.Use` or in the schema's
`Hooks` method) and see the mutation, not the model. Momo's model hooks are typed
functions on the model's metadata, `HookSet`: `BeforeInsert`, `BeforeUpdate`,
`BeforeDelete` and `AfterLoad`, set once at start-up on the `Meta` value. They
receive the model pointer and may change its values. Observing every statement
is `momo.WithHook`, and per-handle rules such as a tenant filter are
[interceptors](../PRIVACY_RULES.md).

```go notest
var authorMeta = momo.Meta[Author]{ /* generated metadata */ Hooks: momo.HookSet[Author]{
	BeforeInsert: func(ctx context.Context, a *Author) error {
		a.Name = strings.TrimSpace(a.Name)
		return nil
	},
}}
```

A model hook runs only on the typed execution methods (`Exec`, `All`, `One` and
so on), not on raw SQL, and an error from a Before hook stops the statement
before any SQL runs. Ent validators, immutable fields and privacy policies are
reported by the importer as `go-side-rule` changes: Momo does not run them.

## Transactions

`client.Tx` in Ent hands you a transactional client that you commit or roll back
yourself. `db.Tx` in Momo takes a function instead: it commits when the function
returns nil and rolls back on an error or a panic. Momo calls the function
exactly once: there is no automatic retry, so retry a serialization failure in
your own code. Use the `tx` handle for every statement inside the function.

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/examples/quickstart/models/author"
)

func rename(ctx context.Context, db *momo.DB, id int64, name string) error {
	return db.Tx(ctx, momo.TxOptions{}, func(tx *momo.Tx) error {
		a, err := momo.Select[models.Author](tx).Where(author.ID.Eq(id)).One(ctx)
		if errors.Is(err, momo.ErrNotFound) {
			return fmt.Errorf("author %d does not exist", id)
		}
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		_, err = momo.Update[models.Author](tx).
			Set(author.Name.Set(name)).
			Where(author.ID.Eq(a.ID)).
			Exec(ctx)
		return err
	})
}

func main() {
	ctx := context.Background()
	pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
	if err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

	if err := rename(ctx, db, 1, "Ada Lovelace"); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}
```

## Migrations

`client.Schema.Create` applies the schema to the database on the spot, and Ent
can also write versioned migration files through Atlas. Momo's migrations are SQL
files that `momo migrate diff` writes from your models, each with a schema
snapshot and a `momo.sum` checksum file:

```sh
momo migrate diff add_authors   # writes <version>_add_authors.up.sql, a snapshot and momo.sum
momo migrate apply              # applies pending files under a lock and records them
momo migrate status
```

If you used Ent's Atlas versioned migrations, the Atlas directory reader
(`importer/history/atlas`, see [importing](../importers.md)) verifies `atlas.sum`
and converts the history so nothing runs twice. A database created with
`client.Schema.Create` has no history file; run `momo migrate baseline` on it
(see [migrations](../migrations.md)).

## Errors

Ent returns errors you test with `ent.IsNotFound`, `ent.IsConstraintError` and
related helpers. Momo classifies database errors into sentinels you compare with
`errors.Is`, never with the error text: `momo.ErrNotFound` for a single-row call
that found nothing, `momo.ErrUniqueViolation` and `momo.ErrForeignKeyViolation`
for constraint failures. `All` returns an empty slice, not an error, when
nothing matches.


# Source: replicas.md

# Read replicas

`WithReplicas` registers read-replica drivers on the primary `DB`.
The primary handle never reads from them. `DB.Replica` with an index returns a handle
whose reads may go to that replica; it returns `ErrUnsupported` when that replica
is not configured, and replicas do not chain.

## What goes to a replica

A statement goes to the replica only when it is clearly a plain read: one
statement that starts with SELECT, WITH, VALUES or TABLE, or with EXPLAIN, its
options (ANALYZE, VERBOSE, a parenthesised list) and then one of those. It must
contain none of these words outside literals, quoted identifiers and
comments: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE, INTO, COPY, CREATE, DROP, ALTER,
TRUNCATE, REFRESH, EXECUTE, CALL, DO, LISTEN, NOTIFY, LOCK, DECLARE, GRANT,
REVOKE, VACUUM, ANALYZE, CLUSTER, REINDEX, COMMENT, SECURITY, IMPORT; no row
lock clause (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR KEY SHARE); none of
the side-effect functions nextval, setval, lastval, set_config, pg_notify,
txid_current, pg_terminate_backend, pg_cancel_backend, lo_import, lo_export,
lo_unlink, dblink_exec, pg_reload_conf, pg_switch_wal,
pg_logical_emit_message, or the advisory-lock functions; and no
dollar-quoted body. A semicolon followed by more text (a second statement) is
refused. Anything else goes to the primary. The list is wide on purpose: a
false positive, for example an unquoted column called comment, only costs a
read on the primary.

These never go to a replica, whatever the handle:

- every write (Exec), and every transaction, including reads inside one;
- INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE with RETURNING;
- locking reads, such as FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
- raw SQL that writes, such as a WITH that contains DML, or a SELECT of
  nextval.

One case cannot be detected: a SELECT that calls a user-defined function which
writes looks like a plain read. Run such a call on the primary handle or inside
a transaction. The classifier is covered by
`TestReplicaRoutesWritesAndLocksToPrimary`.

A statement that goes to the primary because it is not a plain read counts as
a write of the unit of work, so the reads that follow it in the same context
see its effects.

## Combining with other options

`DB.Replica` returns `ErrUnsupported` on a DB built with `WithImplicitTx`:
that option runs every statement in its own primary transaction, so a replica
could never be used. A read on a replica runs outside any transaction, so
`WithTxSetup` does not apply to it. Do not rely on a setting that
`WithTxSetup` installs, such as a row-level-security tenant, for replica reads;
use the primary handle for tenant-scoped reads.

## Reading your own writes

Replicas lag. Pass a context from `NewUnitOfWork` through one request: the
first write made through any handle with that context is recorded, and from
then on reads of a Replica handle in that context go to the primary. Wrap a
context with `AllowStaleReads` to send reads back to the replica after a write
when stale data is acceptable (`TestReadReplicaRouting`).

## When the replica is down

If the replica fails with a connection-class error when a read starts
(connection refused or reset, EOF, a network error, SQLSTATE class 08, 57P01 to
57P03 or 53300), that read runs on the primary
(`TestReplicaFailureFallsBackToPrimary`). Other errors, such as a syntax
error, are returned as they are, and so are errors raised after rows have
started to arrive: there is no retry in the middle of a result set. A cancelled
or expired caller context is never retried.


# Source: testing.md

# Testing applications with momotest

`github.com/azrtydxb/momo/momotest` gives your tests a real PostgreSQL
database, isolated per test, with your project's migrations already applied. It
replaces the hand-written scratch-database helper that every application would
otherwise copy.

Do not mock `momo.DB`, `momo.Tx` or `momo.Querier`. The query builders are the
code under test; the constraints and the SQL are what you want to exercise.

## Setup

1. Point the tests at a server you may create schemas on:

   ```sh
   export MOMO_TEST_POSTGRES_URL=postgres://user:pass@localhost:5432/scratch
   ```

   The value must be a `postgres://` or `postgresql://` URL. Use a database you
   do not mind filling with temporary schemas; a disposable container is
   ideal.

2. Embed the migrations in the package that owns the schema, so the binary and
   its tests share them:

   <!-- docscheck:fragment -->

   ```go
   //go:embed migrations
   var files embed.FS

   func Migrations() fs.FS { sub, _ := fs.Sub(files, "migrations"); return sub }
   ```

3. Keep tests that use the kit behind the `integration` build tag (or one of
   your own), and run them with `-tags integration`. A plain `go test` then
   never touches a database.

When the variable is unset, the test is skipped. Set `MOMO_REQUIRE_INTEGRATION=1`
in CI and the test fails instead, so a misconfigured job cannot pass by skipping
everything. `momotest.WithEnv` reads a different variable.

## One database per test: New

<!-- docscheck:fragment -->

```go
func TestSignup(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()
	db := momotest.New(t, momotest.WithMigrations(app.Migrations()))
	// db is a *momo.DB on a schema no other test can see.
}
```

`New` creates a schema, applies the migrations to it and returns a `*momo.DB`.
When the test ends the pool is closed and the schema is dropped. Code under test
may open and commit its own transactions. Use this mode when it does.

## A rollback per test: NewTx

<!-- docscheck:fragment -->

```go
func TestOverdraft(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()
	tx := momotest.NewTx(t, momotest.WithMigrations(app.Migrations()))
	// tx is a *momo.Tx; everything written through it is gone after the test.
}
```

The migrations are applied once to a template schema, named after a hash of the
migration files, the extension list and the momo version, and kept on the
server between runs. The first `momotest.NewTx` in a test binary builds it (or finds it
ready) under an advisory lock, over a short-lived administrator connection;
after that success the binary remembers it, and each later test only opens its
own small pool and begins a transaction, which is much cheaper than `New`. A
changed migration gets a new template; old `momotest_tpl_*` schemas can be
dropped at any time between runs.

The `Tx` is adopted: `Commit` and `Rollback` on it return an error matching
`momo.ErrAdoptedTx`, so a test cannot make its writes permanent. `tx.Tx` opens
savepoints, so you can test a failing step and keep going. Two limits follow
from using one transaction per test:

- Code that must commit, or that needs two connections to see each other's work,
  belongs in a test that uses `New`.
- Parallel tests do not see each other's rows, but two that insert the same
  unique key wait for each other until one finishes. Give parallel tests
  distinct keys.
- DDL, `TRUNCATE` and `LOCK TABLE` inside a `momotest.NewTx` test take locks that block
  every other parallel test using the same template until this one ends. Run
  such tests with `New`.
- Identity and sequence values are consumed by a rolled-back transaction, so
  never assert a literal generated id; compare with the id that `Insert` read
  back.

## Migrations must stay in their schema

Migrations run in a schema of the test's own, with `public` after it on the
search path. Write them unqualified. `momotest` refuses early, with the file
name, a migration that contains `CREATE SCHEMA`, or `CREATE EXTENSION` for an
extension not listed in `momotest.WithExtensions`: an extension exists once per
database, so it would land in one test's schema and vanish under the others when
that schema is dropped. List extensions in `momotest.WithExtensions` (names are matched
in lower case); they are installed once in `public`.

The check reads the SQL with comments and string literals removed, so a comment
that mentions `create schema` is fine and `CREATE /* x */ EXTENSION foo` is still
caught. Quoted identifiers are kept. Dollar-quoted bodies are checked as code,
because a `DO` block can run `CREATE EXTENSION`: the cost is that text inside a
dollar-quoted string that looks like that statement is also refused, with a
message naming the file. Move such text into a normal string, or list the
extension.

`momotest.NewTx` remembers the result of the check and the template name per migration
`fs.FS` value and extension list. Build the FS once, in a package variable or an
`embed.FS`, so that the files are walked once; an FS rebuilt on every call (such
as `fs.Sub` inside a function) is re-read each time, which still works. Only
successes are remembered, so a failed read fails one test and the next one tries
again. Changing the files behind a remembered FS while the test binary runs, for
example rewriting the directory an `os.DirFS` points at, is not supported.

## Leftover schemas

Cleanup runs in `t.Cleanup`, so a killed test run (`kill -9`, a CI timeout)
can leave `momotest_<hex>` schemas behind. They are harmless but accumulate. Drop
them on a disposable server by recreating it, or with
`DROP SCHEMA momotest_<hex> CASCADE` for each name in `pg_namespace` that matches
`momotest\_%` and is not `momotest_tpl_%`. Template schemas `momotest_tpl_*` are
meant to stay. `momotest` has no sweep helper: it never drops a schema it did
not create in the current test.

## Fixtures: Seed

<!-- docscheck:fragment -->

```go
org := &models.Org{Name: "acme"}
momotest.Seed(t, tx,
	momotest.Insert(org),
	momotest.Insert(&models.User{OrgID: org.ID, Email: "ada@acme.test"}),
)
```

`momotest.Seed` runs its steps in the order given, so list a table before the tables that
reference it. All steps run in one transaction (a savepoint when the querier is
a `*momo.Tx`); if one fails, nothing is kept and the test fails. `Insert` reads
generated columns, such as identity keys, back into the rows you pass, so later
steps can use them. `momotest.Graph` inserts a root with the related rows it includes, as
`momo.CreateGraph` does. A step is any `func(ctx, momo.Querier) error`, so
custom fixtures fit too.

## Fixtures from a file: LoadFixtures

`momotest.LoadFixtures(t, q, path)` inserts the rows of a YAML file into `q`, a
`*momo.DB` or a `*momo.Tx`, for data that is easier to read as a file than as Go
structs. The file maps a table name to a list of rows, and each row maps a column
name to a value:

```yaml
authors:
  - id: 1
    name: Ada
documents:
  - id: 1
    author_id: 1
    title: First
  - id: 2
    author_id: null
    title: Orphan
```

Tables are inserted in file order and the rows of a table in list order, so
list a table before the tables that reference it. Columns are written sorted by
name and a YAML `null` becomes SQL `NULL`. Table and column names are quoted
with `momo.Ident` and every value is a bound argument, so a value is never
spliced into the SQL. A table name is one identifier, with no schema prefix.
A value is a string, integer, float, bool, null, timestamp or `!!binary` (read as
bytes); a nested map or list is refused. `momotest.LoadFixtures` writes plain `INSERT`
statements and is tested on PostgreSQL and SQLite; it has not been run against
MySQL or MariaDB. A file that is not a mapping of
tables to lists of rows, a missing file, and a row the database refuses (a
foreign key to a row that is not there, say) fail the test with a message that
names the file, the table and the row. Each row is its own statement, so rows
before a failing one stay unless you pass a transaction.

## SQLite without a server: sqlitetest

`github.com/azrtydxb/momo/momotest/sqlitetest` gives a test a SQLite database
with sqlite-vec loaded, without a server and without an environment variable:
`sqlitetest.New(t, opts...)` returns a `*momo.DB` on a new file in the test's
own temporary directory. Every call opens a file of its own, so two databases in
one test never see each other's tables and parallel tests do not collide. The
database is closed and the file removed when the test ends. The options go to
`momo.New`, for example `momo.WithHook`, and `momotest.LoadFixtures` fills it like any
other database. The database starts empty: create the tables with your own DDL,
for example `momo.SQLiteVectorType` for a vector column (see
[Vector search](vectors.md)); `momotest.WithMigrations` and `momotest.NewTx` are
PostgreSQL features and do not apply.

SQLite lives in its own package, and not in `momotest`, because the SQLite
driver is compiled from C sources: a test binary that imports only `momotest`
for PostgreSQL does not build them, and a repository test
(`TestMomotestAvoidsSQLite`) keeps it that way. Only a test that imports
`sqlitetest` pays for them. The driver needs cgo and a non-Windows target; on
any other build `sqlitetest.New` skips the test, the way `momotest.New` skips
when the server URL is unset.

## Asserting the SQL: AssertSQL

`momotest.AssertSQL(t, compiled, want)` compares the SQL text of a compiled
statement with `want`, ignoring differences in whitespace. Get `compiled` from
the `SQL` method of any query (`Select`, `Insert`, `Update`, `Delete`, a raw
subquery source); the statement is only compiled, never sent, so the assertion
needs no database and the recording hook sees no statement. Because only the
text is compared, put the values in the query and the text in `want`:

```text
c, err := momo.Select[User](db).Where(user.Email.Eq("a@example.test")).SQL()
momotest.AssertSQL(t, c, `SELECT ... FROM "users" WHERE "users"."email" = $1`)
```

On a mismatch the failure holds both texts and `Compiled.String()`, which lists
the bound arguments by placeholder (`$1, $2 bound`). It never holds an argument
value, so a value bound from a `sensitive` column cannot reach the test log.

## Asserting index use: AssertUsesIndex

`momotest.AssertUsesIndex(t, q, compiled, "index_name")` runs a plain `EXPLAIN`
of the statement through `momo.Explain` (never `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, so the
statement is not executed) and fails unless the plan reads that index. It works
on PostgreSQL and SQLite and fails the test on any other dialect.

- PostgreSQL: the index name must be a whole token in an `Index Scan`,
  `Index Only Scan` or `Bitmap Index Scan` node. A name that only starts with
  the asserted one (`orders_idx2` or `orders_idx-old` for `orders_idx`) does
  not match. A mixed-case name that PostgreSQL prints quoted (`"MyIdx"`)
  matches when you pass `MyIdx`.
- SQLite: a plan line must say `USING INDEX name` or
  `USING COVERING INDEX name`.

A failure prints the plan, and says so when the plan contains a sequential scan.
Small tables get sequential scans on PostgreSQL whatever indexes exist: load
enough rows and run `ANALYZE` first, or use `tx.SetLocal(ctx, "enable_seqscan",
"off")`. The database may echo literal values into a plan, so run the assertion
on test data that is not sensitive.

## Listing the SQL: a query registry

An application that leaves a code generator such as sqlc loses its `.sql`
files, which it may lint statically or freeze for compatibility tests against
the previous release. Momo lists the SQL without a database: register each
named query as a builder, then ask the registry for the compiled text per
dialect.

`momo.RegisterQuery(name, build)` adds a query to the process-wide registry
(`momo.DefaultQueries`); `momo.NewQueryRegistry` makes an isolated one for a
test. `build` receives a `momo.Querier` that compiles but never executes (see
`momo.NewOffline`) and returns anything with an `SQL()` method: a `Select`,
`Insert`, `Update`, `Delete` or `Merge` query, or `momo.RawQuery` for a
hand-written statement. Registering a name twice panics, naming the query. The
values you bind in `build` are placeholders and never appear in the listing.
`Registry.Compile(dialect.Postgres)` returns every query sorted by name with
the dialect's placeholders (`$1` on PostgreSQL, `?` on MySQL and SQLite).

`momotest.QueryGolden` writes that list to one golden file per dialect and
fails when a query's SQL changed, a query was added or one was removed. Run the
tests with `MOMO_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1` to accept an intended change, and review the
diff in code review. It needs no database, so it runs in a plain `go test`.

To freeze a release for an N-1 compatibility test, copy its golden file to
`testdata/queries/<release>/postgres.sql`. The program below is the body of
that test: it reads the previous release's file with `momotest.LoadQueryGolden`
and prepares every statement against the current schema, so a dropped column or
table fails the test. `PREPARE` plans a statement without running it, and the
transaction rolls back at the end.

```go
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"log"
	"os"

	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/driver/pgxdriver"
	"github.com/azrtydxb/momo/momotest"
)

func init() {
	momo.RegisterQuery("open_tasks", func(q momo.Querier) momo.Compilable {
		return momo.RawQuery(q, "SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE owner = $1 AND NOT done", 0)
	})
}

func main() {
	if err := run(context.Background()); err != nil {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}

func run(ctx context.Context) error {
	previous, err := momotest.LoadQueryGolden("testdata/queries/v1.4/postgres.sql")
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	pool, err := pgxdriver.NewPool(ctx, os.Getenv("MOMO_EXAMPLE_DSN"))
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	db := momo.New(pgxdriver.New(pool))

	return db.Tx(ctx, momo.TxOptions{}, func(tx *momo.Tx) error {
		for i, q := range previous {
			stmt := fmt.Sprintf("PREPARE compat_%d AS %s", i, q.SQL)
			if _, err := tx.DriverTx().Exec(ctx, stmt, nil); err != nil {
				return fmt.Errorf("the previous release's query %s fails on the new schema: %w", q.Name, err)
			}
		}
		return nil
	})
}
```

## Options

| Option                           | Effect                                                                                          |
| -------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `momotest.WithMigrations(fs.FS)` | Apply these migrations. The directory needs no `momo.sum`. Without it the database is empty.    |
| `momotest.WithEnv(name)`         | Read the server URL from another variable.                                                      |
| `momotest.WithExtensions(names)` | `CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS` in `public` first; with `vector` the pool registers the codec. |
| `momotest.WithMomoOptions(opts)` | Passed to `momo.New`, for example a hook.                                                       |
| `momotest.WithMaxConns(n)`       | Pool size per test: 4 for `New`, 2 for `momotest.NewTx` by default.                             |

## Concurrency

Every call opens its own connection pool and, in `New`, its own schema, so
`t.Parallel` and `-race` are safe. The one shared step, creating extensions and
building a template, runs under a PostgreSQL advisory lock (keyed by
`hashtext` of the names `momotest:extensions` and `momotest:template`), so tests
in one binary and several test binaries running at once (`go test ./...`)
cooperate. `New` also opens a short administrator connection to create and, at
cleanup, drop its schema. A `momotest.NewTx` test holds one connection for its
transaction, plus the pool's spare. Each parallel test holds a few connections; keep the server's
`max_connections` above the number of parallel tests times the pool size, or
lower the pool with `momotest.WithMaxConns` or the parallelism with `-parallel`.

## Example

[examples/testing](../examples/testing/) runs a small bank-account service
